text: Containment gets the attention, but enrichment is where SOAR automation pays for itself every single day. An analyst opening a fresh incident spends the first few minutes just answering who this user is, how risky they've been, what the asset actually runs, and where the traffic really came from. None of that is judgment -- it's retrieval, and retrieval is exactly what you automate, which is what this lesson builds step by step.

Three enrichment points do most of the work. A user risk score from Entra ID Protection -- low, medium, or high, built from sign-in anomalies and leaked-credential signals. Asset criticality -- whether the affected host is an ordinary workstation or a tier-one domain controller. And geo-IP on any IP entity, compared against where that user normally signs in from.

The risk score comes from a real KQL query against AADUserRiskEvents, pulling the account's most recent classification and the specific detail behind it, like impossible travel or a leaked-credential match. A user already flagged high-risk changes how urgently the rest of the incident deserves attention.

Asset criticality and geo-IP both come from a small enrichment step the playbook calls over HTTP -- here, an Azure Function hit with a simple authenticated GET request that looks the hostname or IP up against an inventory or geolocation service and returns a tier or a country.

All three results land in the same place: a comment written back onto the incident, the same action from Lesson 10, now carrying real content instead of a placeholder. The analyst's very first look at the incident already has the answer, so their time goes toward the decision instead of the lookup.

Nothing in this lesson decided anything -- it only assembled facts and wrote them where a human would see them first. Next lesson is where that distinction matters most: containment actions that actually change system state, and the approval gate that has to sit in front of them.
